objectives.text: Describe how the light-dependent reactions convert light energy into ATP and NADPH.

wiki_page.title: The Light-Dependent Reactions of Photosynthesis
wiki_page.body:
Why this page matters

You'll be able toDescribe how the light-dependent reactions convert light energy into ATP and NADPH — the chemical fuel the plant later uses to build sugar.
Cover firstInside the Chloroplast — especially the thylakoid membrane.
This unlocksThe Calvin Cycle, which spends everything the light reactions make.

A quick hook

A leaf sitting in sunlight is, chemically speaking, catching photons and turning them into a battery. How does a plant store something as fleeting as light? Try to answer before reading on: when a photon hits chlorophyll, where does its energy actually go?

Equip: how the light reactions work

The reactions happen in the thylakoid membrane in four connected steps.

  1. Light excites electrons in Photosystem II.
  2. Those electrons travel down an electron transport chain, pumping protons into the thylakoid space.
  3. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase to make ATP.
  4. Photosystem I re-energizes the electrons to reduce NADP+ into NADPH.

Worked example. Follow one electron: it starts in a chlorophyll molecule in Photosystem II, gets knocked loose by a photon, rides the transport chain (releasing energy that pumps protons), and is finally handed to NADP+ at Photosystem I. The water molecule split at the start is what replaces that lost electron — which is also where the oxygen you breathe comes from.

Rethink: check yourself

Where does the oxygen released by photosynthesis come from?

Show answer

From splitting water (H2O) at Photosystem II to replace the electrons chlorophyll loses. It is a by-product, not something the plant needs.

Evaluate

When you feel ready, take the quiz Week 3 Quiz: The Light Reactions — every question maps back to this objective.

Tailor

If the electron transport chain felt shaky, revisit Cellular Respiration: The Electron Transport Chain — the mechanism is the same idea run in reverse. Ready for more? Read ahead to how ATP and NADPH power the Calvin cycle.
